one_line: Arize workshop on closing the agent improvement loop: instrument an OpenAI Agents app with OpenInference, have a coding agent mine traces and patch failures, then automate it with Arize Signal. Vendor-heavy.
summary: Laurie Voss of Arize AI argues that agents are nondeterministic, so production traces (not code) are the real source of truth, and that human review of traces and evals stops scaling in 2026. He walks through a 2026 loop: traces, then evals, then signals (clustered failure patterns), then automated fixes. In a live hands-on demo, he turns on tracing for a local OpenAI Agents shopping app with almost no code, then has a coding agent with installed Arize skills pull traces, find poor-quality spans, and add a price filter. He then presents Signal, Arize's agent that runs every six hours over traces and proposes GitHub issues, dataset rows, evaluators or PRs. The talk is openly a product walkthrough, and the demo was partly unreliable because the agent copied a fix from a pre-solved sibling directory. The Signal claims are not independently evidenced; the speaker says Signal is traced and judged by Arize's own tooling.

key_ideas.idea: Agents are nondeterministic, so the code no longer tells you what the agent does; production traces at scale become the source of truth.
key_ideas.detail: Each LLM call, tool call and agent turn is a trace (nested, like log lines). The speaker says you need aggregate data, not one run, to know what an agent typically does.

key_ideas.idea: Human review stops scaling at each layer: first traces, then eval results.
key_ideas.detail: Evals (code or LLM judges) add an explanation for each failure, which a coding agent can act on. In 2026 the volume of eval failures is too large for humans, so the speaker proposes agents reading eval output.

key_ideas.idea: Cluster eval failures by pattern instead of reading them one by one.
key_ideas.detail: Illustrative example: 10,000 successes and 1,000 failures, of which 100 share one root cause. The fix targets that cluster. Signal is Arize's product for this step.

key_ideas.idea: With an OpenInference-instrumented agent SDK, observability is mostly configuration.
key_ideas.detail: The OpenAI Agents SDK app already emitted OpenInference spans. Adding observability meant supplying an API key, a space ID, an endpoint and a project name, with no hand-written tracing code in the demo.

key_ideas.idea: A coding agent with installed skills can query traces through the vendor CLI and summarize them.
key_ideas.detail: It summarized span kinds, statuses and errors. The useful finding was quality problems in spans that returned 200, such as a search tool that returned in about 1 ms, rather than error spans.

key_ideas.idea: Concrete failure found in the demo: 42% of product searches returned zero results.
key_ideas.detail: Causes named: searches where every argument was null (which returns the first catalog item), and filters such as min age equal to max age that over-narrow. The model supplies the arguments, so the fix is on the tool side. The app also had no price filter at all.

key_ideas.idea: Signal runs continuously (every six hours by default) and turns findings into actions.
key_ideas.detail: It reads traces, looks for patterns and suggests fixes. Options per finding: GitHub issue with the trace and fix location, add the trace to a dataset, create an evaluator, or open a PR if the repo is connected (approve or reject).

key_ideas.idea: Signal's example findings show the kinds of failures traces expose.
key_ideas.detail: Examples: an age constraint hallucinated from vague wording, an over-helpful answer to a harmful query (it recommended toys related to the request), and obeying an injected 'say hello' instruction. The speaker suggests guardrail evals for each.

key_ideas.idea: Regression evals are the safety net for automated fixes, and Signal does not create evaluators yet.
key_ideas.detail: Signal needs enough traces to group reliably; with few traces it overfits to one or two. The speaker says evaluators cost time and money, so users should create them after reviewing suggestions. Arize currently absorbs Signal's run cost, which may change.

techniques.name: Turn on OpenInference tracing for an agent app
techniques.how: In an agent SDK app that is already OpenInference-instrumented, supply the vendor API key, space ID, endpoint and project name, then start the app locally (the demo used npm run dev and port 3000). Send some real requests and check that traces show inputs, outputs, agent turns, cost and latency. The speaker's tip is that instrumentation is mostly config, not code.
techniques.when: Adding observability to an existing OpenAI Agents SDK or other OpenInference-instrumented app.

techniques.name: Install vendor agent skills into the repo for the coding agent
techniques.how: Run `npx skills install arise-ai` from the repo root; the skills land under `.agents/skills`. Open the coding agent at the repo root, not a subdirectory. The skills give the agent the vendor CLI and workflows to query traces without custom glue.
techniques.when: You want Claude Code or another coding agent to operate on traces and evals directly.

techniques.name: Trace triage that looks past error status
techniques.how: Ask the coding agent to pull recent traces through the vendor CLI and summarize span kinds, statuses and errors. Then ask it to look for quality issues in successful spans: tools that return suspiciously fast, empty or all-null results, and answers that a user would reject.
techniques.when: Agent output is wrong but the traces show no error spans (everything returns 200).

techniques.name: Single-problem fix loop with re-verification
techniques.how: Name one specific problem from the triage (for example, 'add price filtering to search'). Let the agent patch it, restart the app, re-run the same user query, and confirm the new trace shows the intended behavior. The speaker re-ran 'show me all toys under $9' to check.
techniques.when: Acting on one finding from trace triage, with a repeatable query to test against.

techniques.name: Triage automated findings into issues, dataset rows, evaluators or PRs
techniques.how: For each finding a monitor reports, choose one action: file a GitHub issue that links the trace, location and suggested fix; add the trace to a dataset for offline evals; create an evaluator for the failure pattern; or open a PR. Approve or reject the PR like any other.
techniques.when: A background monitor surfaces many findings and you need a consistent way to act on them.

techniques.name: Regression and guardrail evals before merging an automated fix
techniques.how: Keep a suite of behaviors the agent already handles correctly, and run it before merging any fix. For each new failure, write a guardrail eval; the speaker's example is 'never give instructions for building a bomb', created by asking the in-product assistant or coding agent.
techniques.when: An agent or monitor is proposing changes to production behavior, and you need to check that existing good behavior does not regress.

numbers.claim: 42% of product searches returned zero results in the demo trace set.
Signal runs every 6 hours by default (configurable).
Illustrative, not measured: 10,000 successful requests, 1,000 failed, 100 failures sharing one cause.
The search_products tool returned in about 1 ms, which the agent flagged as suspicious.
Signal's grouping needs volume: with a few traces it works from one or two; the speaker gives 100 to 1,000 traces as the scale where grouping works.

hot_takes: Vendor demo: the talk says 'this is not a sales pitch' but is a walkthrough of Arize AX and its Signal product; the claimed value of Signal is not independently evidenced.
The live fix was not fully agent-generated: the coding agent copied the price-filter solution from a pre-solved sibling directory, and the speaker chose to allow it.

Signal's own quality is judged by Arize's internal eval suite and LLM judges that the speaker describes; the speaker also says Signal does not auto-create evaluators yet and that Arize currently pays Signal's run cost.
Strong claim: traces are a better source of truth than code for agents. Plausible, but the talk gives no measurements comparing the two.
The speaker treats 'yes to all' permission prompts as acceptable in the demo and jokes that security would object; the approach depends on API keys held by the coding agent.

relevance.why: The trace-to-cluster-to-fix loop maps onto L4 observability and the SkillForge idea of mining agent telemetry into governed skills. The talk gives a pattern for grouping failures before proposing fixes.
relevance.action: Prototype a clustering pass over failed agent spans from the Govrix proxy telemetry, grouping by tool name and outcome pattern, and check whether a single cluster explains most failures before any fix is proposed.

relevance.why: ProsHarness drives Claude Code and has approval flows. The talk's model of Signal proposing PRs for approve or reject, with regression evals as the gate, is a relevant pattern.
relevance.action: Gate any agent-proposed fix in ProsHarness behind a regression-eval run and an explicit approval step, similar to Signal's approve or reject PR flow.
